analysis.one_liner: Halves the tax rate on investment gains, indexes asset values for inflation, and lets homeowners deduct losses on home sales.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee: introduced September 28, 1995, it received no hearing, committee vote, or floor vote before the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let every taxpayer deduct half of their net capital gains from income, roughly halving the tax owed when stocks, business property, or other investments are sold for a profit. It would also have adjusted the purchase price of stocks and business property held more than a year for inflation, so gains that merely keep pace with rising prices would go untaxed, and it would have allowed homeowners to deduct losses from selling a principal residence. It applied to corporations as well as individuals. The bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee and never received any further recorded action.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and corporations with taxable investment gains, especially those with large gains. Taxable capital gains are concentrated among higher-income households, so the 50 percent deduction and inflation indexing would deliver by far their largest dollar benefit to the wealthiest investors. Investors in mutual funds and real estate trusts would benefit through special pass-through rules, and the small minority of homeowners who sell a residence at a loss would gain a new deduction.

how_it_helps.text: Allows every taxpayer to deduct 50 percent of net capital gains from income, roughly halving the effective tax rate on investment profits.
Indexes the purchase price of corporate stock and business property held more than one year to inflation, so gains that only reflect rising prices are not taxed.
Allows an itemized deduction for losses from the sale or exchange of a principal residence, which under current law is not deductible.

Applies the capital gains deduction to corporate taxpayers as well as individuals, and includes pass-through rules so mutual funds, real estate trusts, partnerships, and S corporations can pass the benefit to their investors.

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury, and ultimately taxpayers who do not have large investment gains. Halving the tax on capital gains and indexing asset values would reduce federal revenue, which must be made up through higher deficits or lower spending and higher taxes elsewhere.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal revenue that funds public services

drawbacks.text: Because taxable capital gains are concentrated among higher-income households, most of the tax cut would go to those with the largest investment profits, while the lost revenue would have to be made up through deficits or cuts elsewhere.
The bill repeals the existing 50 percent exclusion for gains on certain small-business stock, eliminating one targeted break to help pay for the broader cut.
Indexing every stock and business asset to inflation would add significant record-keeping and compliance complexity for investors and the tax system.
The homeowner benefit is narrow: losses on home sales are uncommon in practice, so the new deduction would help relatively few people.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Middle-class savers with taxable investments and the rare homeowner who sells at a loss would get real but modest help. The dominant effect, however, is a large tax cut on investment gains, which accrue disproportionately to the wealthiest households and to corporations, paid for with lower federal revenue. Someone concerned about deficits or about who captures tax benefits would see the cost as outweighing the widely shared gains.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and sat there; the record shows no hearing, committee vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Connie Mack introduced the bill in the Senate on September 28, 1995.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
No further action was recorded: the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal revenue was not reduced, and no tax cut flowed to holders of large investment gains. Investors who would have benefited from the half-rate deduction and inflation indexing are worse off than they would have been under the bill; everyone else is spared the cost.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal revenue — the tax cut never happened

for.name: Sen. Connie Mack, III
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Republicans — Senator Mack plus three Republican cosponsors [S4] — but the bill never reached a vote, so no one ever had to take a recorded position on it.

industries.industry: Wealthy holders of stocks and investment assets
industries.note: The 50 percent deduction and inflation indexing would roughly halve the tax on investment gains, and taxable capital gains are concentrated among the wealthiest households. The cost is foregone federal revenue that would otherwise fund services or hold down other taxes.
The deduction applies to corporate as well as individual taxpayers, cutting the tax corporations owe on capital gains. The public bears the revenue loss.

industries.industry: Mutual funds and real estate investment trusts
industries.note: Special rules let regulated investment companies and REITs apply the deduction and indexing at the fund level and pass the benefit through to their investors, including small savers.
REIT investors would get inflation indexing, and homeowners who sell a principal residence at a loss would gain a new deduction — though such losses are uncommon, so this helps relatively few people.
